sweep_summary: Hungarian (hung1274) is in the catalog as fixed-strict initial stress (Siptár & Törkenczy 2000). Of the 22 title-hits, 18 are sentence-prosody / syntax-prosody-interface works (nuclear stress, focus, scope, intonation), 3 are verse metrics or garbled records, and 2 (Blaho & Szeredi, ATOH 12 and WCCFL 28 versions) are about word-level secondary stress. Seven open copies were downloaded and read (Blaho & Szeredi WCCFL 28; Genzel, Ishihara & Surányi 2015 ms; Gyuris & Jackson 2018; Bácskai-Atkári 2013; Hracs 2011 thesis; and the full REAL-J scans of Acta Linguistica Hungarica 39 (1989) and 46 (1999) containing Kenesei & Vogel 1989 and Hunyadi 1999). Four of these state first-hand that word stress is on the initial syllable (Kenesei & Vogel 1989: 161, 'one stress per word, on the first syllable.. compounds.. the first member is the one that bears the stress'; Hunyadi 1999: 76; Genzel et al. 2015 sect. 2.2.2; Blaho & Szeredi 2011: 51) — all confirm the catalog. Blaho & Szeredi refine the catalog's note on trochaic secondary stress: their pilot acoustic study finds no support for either the binary-trochaic (Kerek 1971/Hayes 1995) or the quantity-sensitive (Szinnyei 1912) pattern and argue Hungarian has no metrical secondary stress, only morphosyntactic ones (compound second members, deaccented words, polysyllabic function words). Two already-on-disk sources (Szende 1994 JIPA p. 93; Vogel 2020 ATOH 16) also confirm exceptionless initial stress. Nothing read supersedes Siptár & Törkenczy 2000. Not obtainable: Varga 2002 Intonation and Stress (ch. 6 'Stress in Hungarian Words, Phrases and Sentences', DOI 10.1057/9780230505827_6) — high priority, the fullest English statement of primary and secondary stress; Varga 1998 Phonology and Varga 1983 Folia Linguistica — medium; the ATOH 12 version of Blaho & Szeredi — medium; Mycock 2010, Hunyadi 1996/2002, Ishihara & Ürögdi 2011, Surányi et al. 2012 (abstract only), Jackson et al. 2008, Gyuris et al. 2013 talk, Kerek 1971 (archive.org lending-only), Peperkamp (garbled record), Horváth 2009 — low or none. Benjamins, Springer, Wiley, ScienceDirect and real.mtak.hu (Anubis) blocked non-browser downloads. (with md5sums).

new_statements.quote: The topic field and the comment can be divided prosodically: the elements in the topic field exhibit a rising intonation pattern, constituting a preparatory section to the first obligatory stress, which falls on the first (content) word of the comment, starting a falling intonation pattern. This main stress can be followed by other main stresses in a sequence of downsteps (in a level-prosody sentence). The verb can lose its stress, cliticizing onto the element in the prominent preverbal position (verbal modifier, negative word, etc.). The first obligatory stress can also be followed by a so called eradicating stress (a sharp falling pitch accent) on the element in the prominent preverbal position

new_statements.relation_note: Compatible with the catalog's fixed initial word stress but silent on word-internal placement; it adds the phrase/sentence domain (stress on the first content word of the comment, verb destressing after a verbal modifier, eradicating stress on focus). No contradiction.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Sentence-level only: the first obligatory (main) stress of a Hungarian sentence falls on the first content word of the comment; further main stresses follow in downsteps in level-prosody sentences; the finite verb can lose its stress and cliticize onto the preverbal element; an 'eradicating' stress (sharp falling pitch accent) on the focus/PPP element deaccents or reduces everything after it. The paper does not state where stress falls within a word.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not discussed at word level; at sentence level, post-focal material is 'deaccented, or all other main stresses are reduced'.
new_statements.exceptions: The verb loses its stress when a verbal modifier or negative word occupies the prominent preverbal position (p. 217).
new_statements.identity_note: All opened material describes standard Hungarian; no dialect is named. Peperkamp 1996's stress data are from three languages spoken in Italy, not Hungarian.

new_statements.quote: § 7. Der Hauptton ruht in einem alleinstehenden Worte auf der ersten Silbe. In längeren Wörtern fällt außerdem ein Nebenton auf die dritte und fünfte oder (wenn die dritte kurz ist) auf die vierte und sechste Silbe, aber nie auf die letzte, z. B. arany ‚Gold, Goldstück‘ [å·råń], mindënik ‚jeder, -e, -es‘ [mi·ndenik], aranyakat ‚Goldstücke‘ [å·råńå:kåt], mindëniket ‚jeden, -e, -es‘ [mi·ndeni:kät], kereskëdelëm ‚Handel‘ [kä·räš-kedä:lem]. [Fn. 1:] Der Punkt über der Zeile bezeichnet den Hauptton, der Doppelpunkt den Nebenton. § 8. Unter dem Einfluß des Satztons treten oft Veränderungen in der Betonung der einzelnen Wörter ein.
new_statements.translation: § 7. In a word standing alone the main stress rests on the first syllable. In longer words a secondary stress additionally falls on the third and fifth syllable, or (if the third is short) on the fourth and sixth, but never on the last, e.g. arany 'gold, gold coin' [å·råń], mindënik 'each' [mi·ndenik], aranyakat 'gold coins' [å·råńå:kåt], mindëniket 'each (acc.)' [mi·ndeni:kät], kereskëdelëm 'trade' [kä·räš-kedä:lem]. [Fn. 1:] The point above the line marks the main stress, the colon the secondary stress. § 8. Under the influence of sentence stress, changes often occur in the stress of individual words.

new_statements.relation_note: Agrees with the catalog record (gordon < Siptár & Törkenczy 2000: single primary stress on the initial syllable, fixed-strict) and with Kenesei & Vogel 1989 (one stress per word, first syllable). Adds an early (1912) explicit secondary-stress rule: Nebenton on 3rd/5th or, if the 3rd is short, 4th/6th, never final — i.e. a quantity-conditioned version of the 'regular trochaic pattern of secondary stresses' that the catalog quote says has been 'repeatedly claimed' and that Blaho & Szeredi 2011 found no phonetic evidence for. Primary placement identical; no contradiction.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary stress (Hauptton) falls on the first syllable of a word spoken in isolation. Longer words carry additional secondary stresses (Nebenton) on the 3rd and 5th syllables, or on the 4th and 6th when the 3rd syllable is short; the final syllable is never stressed. In connected speech, sentence stress regroups words into Sprechtakte (stress groups) whose first syllable is usually main- or secondary-stressed while the rest are unstressed (§ 8, p. 12-13).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Yes, explicit: rhythmic secondary stress on odd-numbered non-initial syllables (3rd, 5th), shifted to 4th and 6th if the 3rd syllable is short (a quantity-sensitive alternation), never on the last syllable; examples aranyakat [å·råńå:kåt] and mindëniket [mi·ndeni:kät] (Nebenton on 3rd), kereskëdelëm [kä·räš-kedä:lem] (Nebenton on 4th because 3rd 'ke' is short).
new_statements.exceptions: No lexical exceptions to initial main stress. § 8: under sentence stress the stress of individual words often changes; sentences fall into Sprechtakte in which two or more words unite into one phonetic word, only the first syllable of each Sprechtakt being (main- or secondary-) stressed, e.g. [ä ńńimostå | do:lgom || hod' | å·stšemtudom || ho:lallå | fä:jäm] (p. 13).
new_statements.identity_note: Standard literary Hungarian of 1912 (Budapest norm); Szinnyei's transcription distinguishes closed ë from open e, an orthoepic distinction not made in standard spelling, but the work is not a description of a regional dialect.

sources.quote: Each word in a sentence will be considered to have one stress only (i.e. every phonological word has already undergone metrical reduction on the level of syllable structure). Since Hungarian is a left prominent language (word stress falls on the initial syllable and the first element of compounds carries main stress), column formation will proceed from right to left.
sources.note: Sentence-prosody (metrical-grid) paper; states in passing that word stress is initial and that the first element of a compound carries the main stress. Agrees with catalog fixed: initial syllable coding.

sources.citation: Genzel, Susanne, Shinichiro Ishihara & Balázs Surányi (2015). The prosodic expression of focus, contrast and givenness: A production study of Hungarian. Lingua 165, 183-204. [read: author ms. v3.0, 8 July 2014, REAL repository]
sources.quote: It is relatively uncontroversial that prosodic words are left-headed in Hungarian (Varga 2002), since word stress in Hungarian is always assigned to the initial syllable. The phonological phrase, assumed by definition to contain exactly one pitch accented syllable (Ladd 2008, Féry and Samek-Lodovici 2006), has also been described as being left-headed (Szendrői 2003; cf. Varga 2002).
sources.note: Focus-prosody production study; states (citing Varga 2002) that word stress is always initial. Confirms fixed: initial syllable coding.

sources.citation: Blaho, Sylvia & Dániel Szeredi (2011). Secondary stress in Hungarian: (Morpho)-syntactic, not metrical. In M. B. Washburn et al. (eds.), Proceedings of the 28th West Coast Conference on Formal Linguistics, 51-59. Somerville, MA: Cascadilla.
sources.quote: It is generally accepted that Hungarian has initial primary stress. As for secondary stress, Varga (2000) distinguishes the following four types: 1. first syllable of the second member of a compound 2. first syllable of a deaccented word 3. first syllable of a polysyllabic function word 4. odd non-initial syllable of a non-compound stressed for metrical reasons [...] The most widely cited view, originating from (Hayes, 1995: 330), citing Kerek (1971), is that the language displays a very basic quantity-insensitive left-to-right trochaic foot assignment [...] Therefore these patterns are better explained without proposing the existence of secondary stress in Hungarian.
sources.note: Primary stress initial (uncontroversial). Pilot acoustic study (intensity, F0, duration) of 7 long words: no support for either the binary trochaic (Kerek/Hayes) or the quantity-sensitive (Szinnyei 1912) secondary-stress pattern; speakers have no intuitions and no phonological rule is sensitive to it. Refines the catalog's note that trochaic secondary stress has been 'repeatedly claimed': the empirical evidence is against metrical secondary stress; only the (morpho)syntactic secondary stresses (compound second members, deaccented words, function words) are real.
